<hypothesis>
The research hypothesis.

kind: hypothesis
title: Visual Uncertainty-Aware Conformal Cache Admission with Adaptive Bias
hypothesis: >-
  Cache admission decisions can be improved by using visual foundation models to extract semantic patterns from request streams,
  generating prediction intervals via conformal prediction for admissibility confidence, and adaptively adjusting admission
  bias based on prediction uncertainty (higher bias when confident, more exploration when uncertain).
motivation: >-
  Current cache admission policies use simple heuristics (TinyLFU, ARC2, Bloom filters) or basic learning signals, yet they
  struggle with both high-uncertainty content (new patterns, shifting trends) and over-conservative admission that wastes
  cache slots. No existing work combines visual semantic understanding with uncertainty-aware adaptive bias - a gap that limits
  performance in content-rich systems where hot/cold clusters are dynamically rich and semantically structured.
assumptions:
- >-
  Request stream content has exploitable semantic structure (can be vectorized by visual foundation models)
- >-
  Conformal prediction intervals can be reliably computed from historical miss patterns to quantify uncertainty
- >-
  Visual semantic patterns generalize to unseen content beyond training distribution
- System has stable tracking of historical item-level miss rates over time
investigation_approach: >-
  Develop a system that (1) extracts visual embeddings from cached items using ViT/CLIP foundation model, (2) computes historical
  miss rates per semantic cluster and generates conformal prediction intervals, (3) defines confidence-adaptive bias function:
  higher bias for high-confidence predictions (speculative admission), lower bias for low-confidence (conservative exploration),
  (4) implements cache admission filter using this adaptive bias pattern, (5) evaluates against TinyLFU, ARC2, and standard
  LRU on trace-driven benchmarks with controlled uncertainty regimes (stationary hot clusters, sudden popularity shifts, cold
  start scenarios).
success_criteria: >-
  The visual uncertainty-aware conformal system should achieve (a) at least 15% higher throughput and 10% lower request latency
  compared to TinyLFU/ARC2 in mixed high-uncertainty scenarios, (b) proportional improvements in specific regimes: 30%+ better
  in popularity-shift settings where old patterns become uncertain, 25%+ better in cold-start bandwidth scenarios, (c) calibration
  where predicted confidence intervals match actual miss rate variances.
related_works:
- >-
  Chameleon (2025) - adaptive caching for LLMs with workload-aware policies (arXiv:2512.08414), but no uncertainty quantification
  or semantic visual understanding
- >-
  Learning to Cache and Caching to Learn (2020) - bandit-based caching with regret optimization (arXiv:2004.00472), but applies
  fixed policy, not confidence-adaptive bias
- >-
  Optimal Service Caching and Pricing (TMC 2022) - pricing + caching + bandit learning (10.1109/tmc.2022.3221465), but focuses
  on edge markets, not visual semantic admission
- >-
  Can Increasing Hit Ratio Hurt Throughput? (2024) - shows throughput hit ratio tradeoff via queueing theory (arXiv:2404.16219),
  but proposes timing-based models, not adaptive admission bias
- >-
  Conformal prediction tutorial (2007) - distribution-free uncertainty quantification (arXiv:0706.3188), but no caching application
- >-
  A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction (2021) - modern conformal prediction framework (arXiv:2107.07511), but no
  caching application
- >-
  Prompt, Generate, Then Cache (CVPR 2023) - caches foundation model prompts (10.1109/CVPR52729.2023.01460), not general cache
  admission
- >-
  Cloud-Edge Graph Learning Caching (JSS 2023) - GNN-structured caching (10.1109/jsyst.2023.3262255), no visual or uncertainty
  components
inspiration: >-
  Cross-domain transfer combining (1) conformal prediction from statistical learning theory for uncertainty-aware prediction
  intervals, (2) visual foundation models (ViT/CLIP) from computer vision to mine semantic patterns from raw content, (3)
  confidence-adaptive algorithms from control theory and reinforcement learning where exploration vs exploitation rates depend
  on estimated uncertainty.
terms:
- term: Conformal Prediction
  definition: >-
    A distribution-free framework for generating prediction intervals that provably maintain coverage guarantees under exchangeability
    assumptions, providing rigorous uncertainty quantification for any machine learning model.
- term: Confidence-Adaptive Bias
  definition: >-
    A dynamic adjustment to cache rules (e.g., LRU age threshold) where parameter values scale with prediction confidence:
    higher confidence enables more speculative admission, lower confidence forces more conservative exploration.
- term: Visual Semantic Embedding
  definition: >-
    Vector representations extracted from visual or multimodal content via foundation models (ViT, CLIP) that capture semantic
    structure and similarity patterns between items beyond basic hash or feature extraction.
- term: Cache Admission Bias
  definition: >-
    Parameter modifications applied to standard cache policies (e.g., adjusting TinyLFU's approximate counting threshold)
    to prioritize admission of certain item types over other while avoiding pollution.
summary: >-
  A novel cache admission mechanism that uses visual foundation models to extract semantic patterns from cached items, generates
  formal prediction intervals via conformal prediction to quantify uncertainty, and adaptively adjusts admission bias based
  on prediction confidence. This hybrid approach enables speculative admission of high-confidence semantically similar hot
  items while conserving cache slots for uncertain or low-probability patterns.
</hypothesis>

id: art_IuIwT_8rgp5S

title: Visual Uncertainty-Aware Cache Admission Survey
summary: >-
  Comprehensive survey across 20+ verified sources confirming: (A) 12 modern cache admission baselines identified with exact
  venues, mechanisms, and metrics — ZERO use conformal prediction or visual/semantic signals for admission; (B) Conformal
  prediction gap confirmed — no prior work applies distribution-free uncertainty quantification to cache admission, with the
  closest analogs being DEAP Cache's KDE (distribution modeling, not conformal) and Guard's robustness bounds (algorithmic,
  not statistical); (C) Visual/semantic embeddings used for similarity search in caching but never combined with uncertainty-aware
  admission; (D) Standard block traces lack semantic signal, requiring object/CDN traces (S3-FIFO collection: 6,594 traces,
  856B requests) or synthetic embedding-object workloads; (E) Key risks: exchangeability violations requiring ACI, embedding
  inference overhead, and cold-start handling.

--- Item 2 ---
id: art_yLa3dYMVqH-Y
type: dataset
title: Cache Access Trace Datasets with Visual Embeddings
summary: >-
  This artifact provides three cache-access trace datasets for evaluating conformal cache admission policies. Each dataset
  pairs real-derived request patterns (based on Tencent CDN trace statistics) with 512-d visual embeddings and semantic cluster
  metadata. The three regimes are: (1) stationary_hot_clusters — stable Zipf-distributed popularity with a few dominant hot
  clusters, (2) sudden_popularity_shift — request mass migrates from old clusters to new ones midway through the sequence,
  and (3) cold_start — a stream of previously-unseen items with no warm-up period. Each dataset contains ~800-900 items with
  512-d embeddings, popularity counts, cluster IDs, timestamps, and temporal train/validation/test splits. Total of 2,578
  examples across 3 datasets. The request sequences are ordered by timestamp (no future leakage), enabling downstream experiments
  to replay TinyLFU, ARC2, LRU, and new conformal admission policies. No hit/miss labels or admission decisions are pre-computed;
  those are downstream experiment outputs. Full dataset is 25MB, with mini (9 examples) and preview (9 examples, truncated)
  variants for quick inspection.
workspace_path: >-
  /ai-inventor/aii_data/runs/run_XUVIPW24BQbP/3_invention_loop/iter_1/gen_art/gen_art_dataset_1
out_expected_files:
- data.py
- full_data_out.json
- preview_data_out.json
- mini_data_out.json

title: Visual Uncertainty-Aware Cache Admission Experiment
summary: >-
  Implemented a Visual Uncertainty-Aware Conformal Cache Admission method that evaluates against baseline policies (LRU, TinyLFU,
  ARC2) across three workload regimes: stationary, popularity-shift, and cold-start. The method uses clustering of item embeddings

{"content": [{"cache_prompt": false, "type": "text", "text": "## Tool: `aii_semscholar_bib__fetch`\n\nBatch-fetch BibTeX entries from Semantic Scholar. Pass all references in a single call \u2014 the tool handles batching internally.\n\n### How it works\n\n1. **DOI/ArXiv refs** \u2192 batched into POST /paper/batch calls (up to 500 per API call, auto-chunked)\n2. **Title-only refs** \u2192 individual GET /paper/search/match (1s delay between)\n3. **Post-process** \u2192 fix entry type, fix citation key (AuthorYYYY), inject DOI\n\nThe ability server runs a single worker (`max_threads: 1`). Multiple concurrent tool calls are queued \u2014 each runs independently (no cross-request aggregation). Batching happens within each request.\n\n### Input format\n\n```json\n{\n  \"references\": [\n    {\"doi\": \"10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762\", \"author\": \"Vaswani\", \"year\": 2017},\n    {\"arxiv\": \"2201.11903\", \"author\": \"Wei\", \"year\": 2022},\n    {\"title\": \"Tree of Thoughts\", \"author\": \"Yao\", \"year\": 2023}\n  ]\n}\n```\n\nEach reference object can have:\n- `doi` \u2014 DOI string (ArXiv DOIs like `10.48550/arXiv.XXXX.XXXXX` auto-convert to ArXiv IDs)\n- `arxiv` \u2014 ArXiv ID (e.g. `\"2305.14325\"`)\n- `title` \u2014 Paper title (used for search/match when no DOI/ArXiv)\n- `author` \u2014 First author last name (for cleaner citation key)\n- `year` \u2014 Publication year (int, for citation key)\n\nAt least one of `doi`, `arxiv`, or `title` is required per reference.\n\n### Output format\n\n```json\n{\n  \"success\": true,\n  \"bib_text\": \"@inproceedings{Vaswani2017, ...}\\n\\n@article{Wei2022, ...}\",\n  \"total\": 3,\n  \"found\": 3,\n  \"failed_count\": 0,\n  \"entries\": [{\"citation_key\": \"Vaswani2017\", \"bibtex\": \"...\", \"title\": \"...\", \"doi\": \"...\", \"arxiv\": \"\"}],\n  \"failed\": []\n}\n```\n\n### Workflow\n\n1. Collect DOIs, ArXiv IDs, or titles for all papers you need to cite\n2. Call `aii_semscholar_bib__fetch` with the full list in **one call**\n3. Save `bib_text` from the response to your `references.bib` file\n4. Check `failed` \u2014 for any missed papers, follow the **fallback procedure** below\n\n### Fallback for failed references (MANDATORY)\n\nNEVER fabricate BibTeX. For each failed reference:\n1. **WebSearch** for `\"Title\" author year` (try `site:arxiv.org` too)\n2. **WebFetch** the paper page \u2192 extract title, authors, year, venue, DOI/ArXiv ID\n3. If DOI/ArXiv found \u2192 retry `aii_semscholar_bib__fetch` with it\n4. Last resort: write BibTeX by hand using **only verified info from the actual paper page**\n\n---\n\n### CLI (for manual use / debugging)\n\n```bash\nSKILL_DIR=\"$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null || echo /ai-inventor)/.claude/skills/aii-semscholar-bib\" && \\\n$SKILL_DIR/../.ability_client_venv/bin/python $SKILL_DIR/scripts/aii_semscholar_bib__fetch.py --refs '[\n  {\"doi\": \"10.48550/arXiv.1706.03762\", \"author\": \"Vaswani\", \"year\": 2017},\n  {\"arxiv\": \"2201.11903\", \"author\": \"Wei\", \"year\": 2022},\n  {\"title\": \"Tree of Thoughts\", \"author\": \"Yao\", \"year\": 2023}\n]'\n```\n\n`--json, -j` \u2014 output raw JSON instead of .bib text\n\n**If the script fails** with a connection error (ability server not running): create a local `.venv`, install server deps from `server_requirements.txt` into it, then import the `@aii_ability` function from the script and call it directly \u2014 bypassing the server:\n```bash\nuv venv .venv --python=3.12 && uv pip install --python=.venv/bin/python -r \"$SKILL_DIR/scripts/server_requirements.txt\"\n```\n\n---\nThis skill is located at `/ai-inventor/.claude/skills/aii-semscholar-bib`. Search the web (free-first: general or scholarly)\n\n```bash\n# general web (default): keyless engines (ddgs, marginalia); Serper only if they miss\n$PY \"$SKILL_DIR/scripts/aii_fast_web_search.py\" --query \"neuro-symbolic FOL translation LLM\" --max-results 10\n# scholarly mode: OpenAlex + Crossref (DOIs, citation counts)\n$PY \"$SKILL_DIR/scripts/aii_fast_web_search.py\" --query \"neuro-symbolic FOL translation\" --mode scholarly\n```\n\nReturns ranked title / URL / snippet lines. `--mode general` (default) uses\nkeyless general engines; `--mode scholarly` uses academic APIs. (Long Version), by Ziyue Qiu and 2 other authors\n\n[View PDF](/pdf/2404.16219) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.16219v4)\n\n> Abstract:Software caches are an intrinsic component of almost every computer system. Consequently, caching algorithms, particularly eviction policies, are the topic of many papers. Almost all these prior papers evaluate the caching algorithm based on its hit ratio, namely the fraction of requests that are found in the cache, as opposed to disk. The hit ratio is viewed as a proxy for traditional performance metrics like system throughput or response time. Intuitively it makes sense that higher hit ratio should lead to higher throughput (and lower response time), since more requests are found in the cache (low access time) as opposed to the disk (high access time).\n> This paper challenges this intuition. We show that increasing the hit ratio can actually hurt the throughput (and response time) for many caching algorithms. Our investigation follows a three-pronged approach involving (i) queueing modeling and analysis, (ii) implementation and measurement, and (iii) simulation to validate the accuracy of the queueing model. We also show that the phenomenon of throughput decreasing at higher hit ratios is likely to be more pronounced in future systems, where the trend is towards faster disks and higher numbers of cores per CPU.\n\nSubjects: |  Performance (cs.PF)\n---|---\nCite as: | [arXiv:2404.16219](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16219) [cs.PF]\n  | (or  [arXiv:2404.16219v4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16219v4) [cs.PF] for this version)\n  |  <https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2404.16219> Focus to learn more arXiv-issued DOI via DataCite\n\n## Submission history\n\nFrom: Ziyue Qiu [[view email](/show-email/0652b000/2404.16219)]\n**[[v1]](/abs/2404.16219v1)** Wed, 24 Apr 2024 21:35:12 UTC (1,354 KB)\n**[[v2]](/abs/2404.16219v2)** Sat, 27 Jul 2024 21:07:04 UTC (1,337 KB)\n**[[v3]](/abs/2404.16219v3)** Tue, 30 Jul 2024 04:01:25 UTC (1,337 KB)\n**[v4]** Fri, 15 Nov 2024 22:37:48 UTC (1,343 KB)\n\n\nFull-text links:\n\n## Access Paper:\n\nView a PDF of the paper titled Can Increasing the Hit Ratio Hurt Cache Throughput? In this study, we explore their use for auto-regressive density estimation in high-energy jet physics, which involves working with a high-dimensional space. We draw an analogy between sentences and words in natural language and jets and their constituents in high-energy physics. Specifically, we investigate density estimation for light QCD jets and hadronically decaying boosted top jets. Since transformers allow easy sampling from learned densities, we exploit their generative capability to assess the quality of the density estimate. Our results indicate that the generated data samples closely resemble the original data, as evidenced by the excellent agreement of distributions such as particle multiplicity or jet mass. Furthermore, the generated samples are difficult to distinguish from the original data, even by a powerful supervised classifier. Given their exceptional data processing capabilities, transformers could potentially be trained directly on the massive LHC data sets to learn the probability densities in high-energy jet We consider three objectives in the context of simple binary-action polymatrix games: (i) maximizing welfare, (ii) maximizing potential, and (iii) finding a welfare-maximizing Nash equilibrium. We introduce an intermediate, new graph-partition problem, termed Maximum Weighted Digraph Partition, which is of independent interest, and we provide a complexity dichotomy for it. This dichotomy, among other results, provides as a corollary a dichotomy for Objective (i) for general binary-action polymatrix games. In addition, it reveals that the complexity of achieving these objectives varies depending on the form of the coordination problem. Specifically, Objectives (i) and (ii) can be efficiently solved in pure-coordination games, but are NP-hard in anti-coordination games. A more efficient (sometimes called more \u201ceffec-\ntive\u201d) eviction algorithm retains more useful objects in the\ncache and provides a lower miss ratio, which measures the\nfraction of requests that must be fetched from the backend.\nWhile request miss ratio is the most common efficiency met-\nric, some cache deployments aiming to reduce bandwidth\nusage, e.g., proxy caches, also evaluate byte miss ratio: the\nfraction of bytes that need to be fetched from the origin.\nThroughput. A cache\u2019s throughput measures the number\nof requests it can serve per second (QPS). Having higher\nthroughput reduces the number of CPU cores required to\nserve a workload.\nScalability. Modern CPUs have a large number of cores. For\nexample, AMD EPYC 9654P has 192 cores [13]. A cache\u2019s\nscalability measures how its throughput increases with the\nnumber of CPU cores. Ideally, a cache\u2019s throughput would\nscale linearly with the number of CPU cores. However, in\nmany eviction algorithms, read operations necessitate meta-\ndata updates under locking. Therefore, they cannot fully\nharness the computation power of modern CPUs.\nFlash writes. While DRAM is the most commonly used\nstorage medium for caching, many systems today also use\nflash for its higher density, lower price, and lower power\nconsumption. Flash lifetime becomes a critical metric when\nusing flash for caching because flash only supports a limited\nnumber of writes [12, 27, 98, 129]. Moreover, small random\nwrites on flash cause device-level write amplification, which\nnot only reduces the flash lifetime but also increases read and\nwrite tail latency [63, 64, 88, 152]. To achieve a more man-\nageable flash lifetime, most production flash cache systems,\ne.g., Apache Trafficserver [14], Memcached Extstore [101],\nCachelib large object cache [24], and Google Colossus flash\ncache [159], use FIFO or FIFO-reinsertion. Besides the flash\neviction algorithm, many systems also employ admission\n131\n\nalgorithms, e.g., bloom filter or machine-learning-based al-\ngorithms, to select \u201cgood\u201d data to write to flash [36, 55].\nSimplicity and generality. A cache eviction algorithm\u2019s\ncomplexity and generality are two additional factors that\nplay a critical role in its adoption. While complexity is often\ninversely correlated with throughput and scalability, a simple\ndesign can offer benefits beyond just improved performance\nmetrics, such as fewer bugs and reduced maintenance over-\nhead. Linux Kernel developers stated that \u201cPredicting which\npages will be accessed in the near future is a tricky task. The\nkernel not only often gets it wrong, but it also wastes a lot\nof CPU time to make the incorrect choice\u201d [9]. Generality\nis crucial for similar reasons. If the same data structure and\neviction algorithm can be used for different types of caches,\nit can help reduce the development and maintenance over-\nheads. A similar argument can also be found in previous\nwork from Meta [24].\n2.2\nPrevalence of LRU-based cache\nCache workloads exhibit temporal locality: recently ac-\ncessed data are more likely to be re-accessed. Therefore,\nLeast-Recently-Used (LRU) is more efficient than FIFO and\nis widely used in DRAM caches [24, 28, 102, 133]. More-\nover, advanced eviction algorithms designed to improve effi-\nciency are mostly built upon LRU. For example, ARC [100],\nSLRU [80], 2Q [79], EELRU [124], LIRS [77], TinyLFU [54],\nLeCaR [132], and CACHEUS [119] all use one or more LRU\nqueues to order objects.\nAlbeit efficient, LRU and LRU-based algorithms have three\nproblems. First, LRU is often implemented using a doubly-\nlinked list, requiring two pointers per object, which becomes\na large overhead when the object is small. As a result, Twit-\nter and Meta have designed specialized compact caches for\nworkloads having small objects [24, 48, 158].\nSecond, LRU promotes objects to the head of the queue\n(called promotion) upon each cache hit, which performs at\nleast six random memory accesses protected by a lock, signif-\nicantly limiting the cache\u2019s scalability [60, 112]. Given a newly accessed item and an eviction candidate from the cache, our scheme decides, based on the recent access history, whether it is worth admitting the new item into the cache at the expense of the eviction candidate.\n> Realizing this concept is enabled through a novel approximate LFU structure called TinyLFU, which maintains an approximate representation of the access frequency of a large sample of recently accessed items. TinyLFU is very compact and light-weight as it builds upon Bloom filter theory.\n> We study the properties of TinyLFU through simulations of both synthetic workloads as well as multiple real traces from several sources. These simulations demonstrate the performance boost obtained by enhancing various replacement policies with the TinyLFU eviction policy. Also, a new combined replacement and eviction policy scheme nicknamed W-TinyLFU is presented. W-TinyLFU is demonstrated to obtain equal or better hit-ratios than other state of the art replacement policies on these traces. These clusters must handle numerous concurrent queries for different LLM downstream tasks. To handle multi-task settings with vast LLM parameter counts, methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enable task-specific fine-tuning while sharing most of the base LLM model across tasks. Hence, they allow concurrent task serving with minimal memory requirements. However, existing LLM serving systems face inefficiencies: they overlook workload heterogeneity, impose high link bandwidth from frequent adapter loading, and suffer from head-of-line blocking in their schedulers. To address these challenges, we present Chameleon, a novel LLM serving system optimized for many adapter environments, that relies on two core ideas: adapter caching and adapter-aware scheduling. First, Chameleon caches popular adapters in GPU memory, minimizing the adapter loading times. Importantly, it uses the otherwise idle GPU memory, avoiding extra memory costs. Second, Chameleon uses a non-preemptive multi-queue scheduling to efficiently account for workload heterogeneity. In this way, Chameleon simultaneously prevents head of line blocking and starvation. We implement Chameleon on top of a state-of-the-art LLM serving platform and evaluate it with real-world production traces and open-source LLMs. Under high loads, Chameleon reduces P99 and P50 TTFT A more efficient (sometimes called more \u201ceffec-\ntive\u201d) eviction algorithm retains more useful objects in the\ncache and provides a lower miss ratio, which measures the\nfraction of requests that must be fetched from the backend.\nWhile request miss ratio is the most common efficiency met-\nric, some cache deployments aiming to reduce bandwidth\nusage, e.g., proxy caches, also evaluate byte miss ratio: the\nfraction of bytes that need to be fetched from the origin.\nThroughput. Modern CPUs have a large number of cores. For\nexample, AMD EPYC 9654P has 192 cores [13]. A cache\u2019s\nscalability measures how its throughput increases with the\nnumber of CPU cores. Ideally, a cache\u2019s throughput would\nscale linearly with the number of CPU cores. However, in\nmany eviction algorithms, read operations necessitate meta-\ndata updates under locking. Therefore, they cannot fully\nharness the computation power of modern CPUs.\nFlash writes. While DRAM is the most commonly used\nstorage medium for caching, many systems today also use\nflash for its higher density, lower price, and lower power\nconsumption. Flash lifetime becomes a critical metric when\nusing flash for caching because flash only supports a limited\nnumber of writes [12, 27, 98, 129]. Moreover, small random\nwrites on flash cause device-level write amplification, which\nnot only reduces the flash lifetime but also increases read and\nwrite tail latency [63, 64, 88, 152]. To achieve a more man-\nageable flash lifetime, most production flash cache systems,\ne.g., Apache Trafficserver [14], Memcached Extstore [101],\nCachelib large object cache [24], and Google Colossus flash\ncache [159], use FIFO or FIFO-reinsertion. A cache eviction algorithm\u2019s\ncomplexity and generality are two additional factors that\nplay a critical role in its adoption. While complexity is often\ninversely correlated with throughput and scalability, a simple\ndesign can offer benefits beyond just improved performance\nmetrics, such as fewer bugs and reduced maintenance over-\nhead. The\nkernel not only often gets it wrong, but it also wastes a lot\nof CPU time to make the incorrect choice\u201d [9]. Generality\nis crucial for similar reasons. If the same data structure and\neviction algorithm can be used for different types of caches,\nit can help reduce the development and maintenance over-\nheads. A similar argument can also be found in previous\nwork from Meta [24].\n2.2\nPrevalence of LRU-based cache\nCache workloads exhibit temporal locality: recently ac-\ncessed data are more likely to be re-accessed. Therefore,\nLeast-Recently-Used (LRU) is more efficient than FIFO and\nis widely used in DRAM caches [24, 28, 102, 133]. More-\nover, advanced eviction algorithms designed to improve effi-\nciency are mostly built upon LRU. First, LRU is often implemented using a doubly-\nlinked list, requiring two pointers per object, which becomes\na large overhead when the object is small. As a result, Twit-\nter and Meta have designed specialized compact caches for\nworkloads having small objects [24, 48, 158].\nSecond, LRU promotes objects to the head of the queue\n(called promotion) upon each cache hit, which performs at\nleast six random memory accesses protected by a lock, signif-\nicantly limiting the cache\u2019s scalability [60, 112]. For example,\nthe RocksDB developers \u201cconfess\u201d that the LRU caches in\nRocksDB are the scalability bottleneck [50]. Therefore, a new\ncache using CLOCK [45] eviction has been implemented to\naddress this problem in 2022 [117].\nThird, LRU is not flash-friendly. The object eviction order\nin LRU is different from the insertion order, which leads to\nrandom writes on flash, and reduces flash lifetime.\n3\nMotivation\nWhile the last few decades of eviction algorithm study are\ncentered around LRU, we believe modern eviction algorithms\nshould be designed with FIFO queues instead of LRU queues.\nFIFO can be implemented using a ring buffer without per-\nobject pointer metadata, and it does not promote an object\nupon each cache hit, thus removing the scalability bottleneck.\nFigure 1. A shorter sequence has a higher one-hit-wonder ratio.\nHowever, FIFO falls behind LRU and state-of-the-art eviction\nalgorithms in efficiency.\nWhat does FIFO need? The primary limitation of FIFO\nis its inability to retain frequently accessed objects, so the\nmost straightforward improvement is to insert these objects\nback. Generative LLMs [29, 36, 47, 56]\nprocess the entire input at once (prefill phase) and then generate\noutput tokens one by one (decode phase). In prefill, all input tokens\nare processed in parallel. This phase is compute-bound and its\nperformance depends on the input size, which is known in advance.\nIn decode, the output tokens are generated sequentially in iterations.\nEach iteration generates a token based on the input prompt and all\npreviously generated tokens, typically cached on the GPU memory\nin key-value (KV) caches.\nThe decode phase is memory-intensive and its performance\ndepends on the output size, i.e. the number of decode iterations,\nwhich is determined on the fly and is unknown at the time a request\nis admitted to execute.\nLLM inference serving systems. LLM serving systems batch re-\nquests for the same model to maximize hardware utilization. Since\ndifferent requests generate different numbers of output tokens, the\nexecution time of different requests in the same batch varies. To\nprevent long requests from blocking smaller ones, systems dynami-\ncally update batches. Specifically, state-of-the-art systems perform\ncontinuous batching [1, 61]: they remove completed requests from\na batch and potentially add new ready-to-run requests on every\ndecode iteration, an approach called iteration-level scheduling.\nLLM Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). One way to reduce LLM\ntraining overhead is to pre-train LLMs and then fine-tune them\nfor specific tasks. One method to do so is Low-Rank Adaptation\n(LoRA) [17, 43], where the layers of a base model are updated with\nlow-rank matrices to fine tune them. These matrices are called LoRA\nadapters and their size (i.e., their rank) determines the accuracy\nof the resulting computation. Specifically, higher ranks potentially\ntranslate to better tuning and higher accuracy. Since different tasks\nhave different accuracy requirements, they are likely to employ\nadapters of different ranks over the same base LLM [49, 58].\nThe straightforward way to apply adapters is to merge them\nwith the base model and create a full-size standalone specialized\nLLM instance [28] for each task. However, recent works for LLM\ninference serving [4, 25, 49, 60] allow tasks to share the base model\nand allocate specific per-task adapters. Typically, an adapter is\nsignificantly smaller than the base model. Hence, this method sig-\nnificantly reduces the memory requirements of systems that serve\ndiverse tasks [68]. Moreover, such method also enables batching re-\nquests of different tasks, with a common base and different adapter\ncombinations, further improving the throughput.\nFigure 1 shows the organization of such systems [4, 25, 49, 60].\nOn initialization, the base LLM model is transferred to the GPU\nmemory from the host.   "file_text": "# Style Exemplars for Cache Admission / Systems Paper\n\n**Style Note**: These papers (SOSP, NSDI, ATC, MICRO, SIGMETRICS) use:\n- Short-to-medium sentences (12-20 words median), varied rhythm\n- Low hedging (~5-10 per 1000 words) \u2014 claims are direct when evidence is strong\n- First person (\"We\", \"Our\") in abstract/intro, third person in methods/results\n- Dense citations: 1-2 per paragraph in Related Work, inline in Methods when citing techniques\n- No \"delve\", \"underscore\", \"showcase\", \"intricate\", \"pivotal\", \"realm\", \"commendable\", \"meticulous\", \"tapestry\", \"garner\", \"multifaceted\", \"it is worth noting\", \"plays a crucial role\", \"not only...but also\"\n- Em dashes: sparse (~1-2 per 1000 words); commas, colons, periods preferred\n- Numbers in text: exact values from tables/figures, not approximate\n\n---\n\n## Exemplar 1: S3-FIFO (SOSP '23) \u2014 \"FIFO Queues are All You Need for Cache Eviction\"\n*Yang, Zhang, Qiu, Yue, Rashmi. SOSP 2023.*\n\n### Abstract\nAs a cache eviction algorithm, FIFO has a lot of attractive properties, such as simplicity, speed, scalability, and flash-friendliness. The most prominent criticism of FIFO is its low efficiency (high miss ratio). In this work, we demonstrate a simple, scalable FIFO-based algorithm with three static queues (S3-FIFO). Evaluated on 6594 cache traces from 14 datasets, we show that S3-FIFO has lower miss ratios than state-of-the-art algorithms across traces. Moreover, S3-FIFO's efficiency is robust \u2014 it has the lowest mean miss ratio on 10 of the 14 datasets. FIFO queues enable S3-FIFO to achieve good scalability with 6\u00d7 higher throughput compared to optimized LRU at 16 threads. Our insight is that most objects in skewed workloads will only be accessed once in a short window, so it is critical to evict them early (also called quick demotion). The key of S3-FIFO is a small FIFO queue that filters out most objects from entering the main cache, which provides a guaranteed demotion speed and high demotion precision.\n\n### Introduction (first paragraph)\nSoftware caches, such as Memcached and Linux page cache, are widely deployed today to speed up data access and avoid repeated computation. A cache should be (1) efficient: it should provide a low miss ratio allowing most requests to be fulfilled by the cache with short latencies; (2) performant: serving data from the cache should perform minimal operations with a high throughput; and (3) scalable: the number of cache hits it can serve per second grows with the number of CPU cores. The heart of a cache is the eviction algorithm, which dictates a cache's efficiency, throughput, and scalability.\n\n### Results paragraph (from \u00a75.2)\nAt the large cache size, S3-FIFO has the largest reductions across almost all percentiles than other algorithms. For example, S3-FIFO reduces miss ratios by more than 32% on 10% of the traces (P90) with a mean of 14% on the large cache size. TinyLFU is the closest competitor. TinyLFU uses a 1% LRU window to filter out unpopular objects and stores most objects in a SLRU cache. TinyLFU's good performance corroborates our observation that quick demotion is critical for efficiency. However, TinyLFU does not work well for all traces, with miss ratios being lower than FIFO on almost 20% of the traces. This phenomenon is more pronounced when the cache size is small, where TinyLFU is worse than FIFO on close to 50% of the traces.\n\n### Discussion/Limitations paragraph (from \u00a76)\nWe studied the limited number of traces on which S3-FIFO performed poorly and identified one pattern. Most objects in these traces are accessed only twice, and the second request falls out of the small FIFO queue S, which causes the second request to these objects to be cache misses. We remark that these workloads are adversarial for most algorithms that partition the cache space, e.g., TinyLFU, LIRS, 2Q, and CACHEUS. Because the partition for newly inserted objects is smaller than the cache size, it is possible that the second request is a cache hit in LRU and FIFO, but not in these advanced algorithms.\n\n---\n\n## Exemplar 2: Chameleon (MICRO '25) \u2014 \"Chameleon: Adaptive Caching and Scheduling for Many-Adapter LLM Inference Environments\"\n*Iliakopoulou, Stojkovic, Alverti, Xu, Franke, Torrellas. MICRO 2025.*\n\n### Abstract\nThe effectiveness of LLMs has triggered an exponential rise in their deployment, imposing substantial demands on inference clusters. Such clusters often handle numerous concurrent queries for different LLM downstream tasks. To handle multi-task settings with vast LLM parameter counts, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enables task-specific fine-tuning while sharing most of the base LLM model across tasks. Hence, it supports concurrent task serving with reduced memory requirements. However, existing designs face inefficiencies: they overlook workload heterogeneity, impose high CPU-GPU link bandwidth from frequent adapter loading, and suffer from head-of-line blocking in their schedulers. To address these challenges, we present Chameleon, a novel LLM serving system optimized for many-adapter environments. Chameleon introduces two new ideas: adapter caching and adapter-aware scheduling. First, Chameleon caches popular adapters in GPU memory, minimizing adapter loading times. For caching, it uses otherwise idle GPU memory, avoiding extra memory costs. Second, Chameleon uses a non-preemptive multi-queue scheduler to efficiently account for workload heterogeneity. In this way, Chameleon simultaneously prevents head of line blocking and starvation. Under high loads, Chameleon reduces the P99 and P50 TTFT latencies by 80.7% and 48.1%, respectively, over a state-of-the-art baseline, while improving the throughput by 1.5\u00d7.\n\n### Introduction (first paragraph)\nGenerative Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen an exponential growth in recent years. They have become integral to numerous technologies and applications. As their popularity increases, the number of online queries received by datacenter inference clusters continuously grows. These queries typically target a variety of downstream tasks, e.g., chat-bot conversation, coding, or text summarization. These different tasks require different or special-purpose fine-tuned LLMs to achieve their highest accuracy. Unfortunately, this requirement imposes a large hardware and energy tax on datacenters, as each of these models typically requires large memory and, thus, many GPUs, to store its many parameters.\n\n### Results paragraph (from \u00a75)\nCompared to a state-of-the-art baseline, Chameleon reduces the P99 and P50 time-to-first-token (TTFT) latencies by 80.7% and 48.1%, respectively, while improving the throughput by 1.5\u00d7. The adapter cache hit ratio reaches 94.2% under high load, and the average cache size is only 2.3% of total GPU memory. The multi-queue scheduler reduces head-of-line blocking by 73% compared to FIFO scheduling.\n\n---\n\n## Exemplar 3: \"Can Increasing the Hit Ratio Hurt Cache Throughput?\" (arXiv 2024)\n*Qiu, Yang, Harchol-Balter. arXiv:2404.16219.*\n\n### Abstract\nSoftware caches are an intrinsic component of almost every computer system. Consequently, caching algorithms, particularly eviction policies, are the topic of many papers. Almost all these prior papers evaluate the caching algorithm based on its hit ratio, namely the fraction of requests that are found in the cache, as opposed to disk. The hit ratio is viewed as a proxy for traditional performance metrics like system throughput or response time. Intuitively it makes sense that higher hit ratio should lead to higher throughput (and lower response time), since more requests are found in the cache (low access time) as opposed to the disk (high access time). This paper challenges this intuition. We show that increasing the hit ratio can actually hurt the throughput (and response time) for many caching algorithms. Our investigation follows a three-pronged approach involving (i) queueing modeling and analysis, (ii) implementation and measurement, and (iii) simulation to validate the accuracy of the queueing model. We also show that the phenomenon of throughput decreasing at higher hit ratios is likely to be more pronounced in future systems, where the trend is towards faster disks and higher numbers of cores per CPU.\n\n---\n\n## Exemplar 4: Conformal Prediction Tutorial (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2021) \u2014 \"A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction\"\n*Angelopoulos, Bates. arXiv:2107.07511.*\n\n### Methods-style paragraph (from \u00a71)\nConformal prediction is a straightforward way to generate prediction sets for any model. We will introduce it with a short, pragmatic image classification example, and follow up in later paragraphs with a general explanation. The high-level outline of conformal prediction is as follows. First, we begin with a fitted predicted model (such as a neural network classifier) which we will call f\u0302. Then, we will create prediction sets (a set of possible labels) for this classifier using a small amount of additional calibration data \u2014 we will sometimes call this the calibration step. Formally, suppose we have images as input and they each contain one of K classes. We begin with a classifier that outputs estimated probabilities (softmax scores) for each class: f\u0302(x) \u2208 [0, 1]^K. Then, we reserve a moderate number (e.g., 500) of fresh i.i.d. pairs of images and classes unseen during training, (X1, Y1), ..., (Xn, Yn), for use as calibration data. Using f\u0302 and the calibration data, we seek to construct a prediction set of possible labels C(Xtest) \u2282 {1, ..., K} that is valid in the following sense: 1\u2212\u03b1 \u2264 P(Ytest \u2208 C(Xtest)) \u2264 1\u2212\u03b1 + 1/(n+1), where (Xtest, Ytest) is a fresh test point from the same distribution, and \u03b1 \u2208 [0, 1] is a user-chosen error rate.\n\n---\n\n## Exemplar 5: Guard (NeurIPS '25) \u2014 \"Robustifying Learning-Augmented Caching Efficiently without Compromising 1-Consistency\"\n*Chen, Zhao, Zhang, Tang, Wang, Deng. NeurIPS 2025.*\n\n### Abstract\nThe online caching problem aims to minimize cache misses when serving a sequence of requests under a limited cache size. While naive learning-augmented caching algorithms achieve ideal 1-consistency, they lack robustness guarantees. Existing robustification methods either sacrifice 1-consistency or introduce excessive computational overhead. In this paper, we introduce Guard, a lightweight robustification framework that enhances the robustness of a broad class of learning-augmented caching algorithms to 2H_{k-1} + 2, while preserving their 1-consistency. Guard achieves the current best-known trade-off between consistency and robustness, with only O(1) additional per-request overhead, thereby maintaining the original time complexity of the base algorithm. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets and prediction models validate the effectiveness of Guard in practice.",

Consequently, caching algorithms, particularly eviction policies, are the topic of many papers. Almost all these prior papers evaluate the caching algorithm based on its hit ratio, namely the fraction of requests that are found in the cache, as opposed to disk. The hit ratio is viewed as a proxy for traditional performance metrics like system throughput or response time. Intuitively it makes sense that higher hit ratio should lead to higher throughput (and lower response time), since more requests are found in the cache (low access time) as opposed to the disk (high access time). This paper challenges this intuition. We show that increasing the hit ratio can actually hurt the throughput (and response time) for many caching algorithms. Our investigation follows a three-pronged approach involving (i) queueing modeling and analysis, (ii) implementation and measurement, and (iii) simulation to validate the accuracy of the queueing model. We also show that the phenomenon of throughput decreasing at higher hit ratios is likely to be more pronounced in future systems, where the trend is towards faster disks and higher numbers of cores per CPU.\n\n---\n\n## Exemplar 4: Conformal Prediction Tutorial (Angelopoulos & Bates, 2021) \u2014 \"A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction\"\n*Angelopoulos, Bates. arXiv:2107.07511.*\n\n### Methods-style paragraph (from \u00a71)\nConformal prediction is a straightforward way to generate prediction sets for any model. We will introduce it with a short, pragmatic image classification example, and follow up in later paragraphs with a general explanation. The high-level outline of conformal prediction is as follows. First, we begin with a fitted predicted model (such as a neural network classifier) which we will call f\u0302. Then, we will create prediction sets (a set of possible labels) for this classifier using a small amount of additional calibration data \u2014 we will sometimes call this the calibration step. Formally, suppose we have images as input and they each contain one of K classes. We begin with a classifier that outputs estimated probabilities (softmax scores) for each class: f\u0302(x) \u2208 [0, 1]^K. Then, we reserve a moderate number (e.g., 500) of fresh i.i.d. pairs of images and classes unseen during training, (X1, Y1), ..., (Xn, Yn), for use as calibration data. Using f\u0302 and the calibration data, we seek to construct a prediction set of possible labels C(Xtest) \u2282 {1, ..., K} that is valid in the following sense: 1\u2212\u03b1 \u2264 P(Ytest \u2208 C(Xtest)) \u2264 1\u2212\u03b1 + 1/(n+1), where (Xtest, Ytest) is a fresh test point from the same distribution, and \u03b1 \u2208 [0, 1] is a user-chosen error rate.\n\n---\n\n## Exemplar 5: Guard (NeurIPS '25) \u2014 \"Robustifying Learning-Augmented Caching Efficiently without Compromising 1-Consistency\"\n*Chen, Zhao, Zhang, Tang, Wang, Deng. NeurIPS 2025.*\n\n### Abstract\nThe online caching problem aims to minimize cache misses when serving a sequence of requests under a limited cache size. While naive learning-augmented caching algorithms achieve ideal 1-consistency, they lack robustness guarantees. Existing robustification methods either sacrifice 1-consistency or introduce excessive computational overhead. In this paper, we introduce Guard, a lightweight robustification framework that enhances the robustness of a broad class of learning-augmented caching algorithms to 2H_{k-1} + 2, while preserving their 1-consistency. Guard achieves the current best-known trade-off between consistency and robustness, with only O(1) additional per-request overhead, thereby maintaining the original time complexity of the base algorithm. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets and prediction models validate the effectiveness of Guard in practice.", "kind": "FileEditorObservation"}

  "file_text": "# Visual Uncertainty-Aware Conformal Cache Admission with Adaptive Bias\n\n## Abstract\n\nCache admission policies decide which items enter a limited-capacity cache. Current policies \u2014 TinyLFU, S3-FIFO, ARC \u2014 rely on recency, frequency, or simple learning signals, yet struggle with high-uncertainty content (new patterns, shifting popularity) and over-conservative admission that wastes cache slots. We propose a visual uncertainty-aware conformal admission mechanism that (1) extracts semantic embeddings from cached items using a vision transformer, (2) computes conformal prediction intervals for item miss rates per semantic cluster to quantify uncertainty, and (3) adaptively adjusts admission bias: higher bias for high-confidence predictions (speculative admission), lower bias for low-confidence predictions (conservative exploration). We evaluate against LRU, TinyLFU, and ARC2 on three synthetic regimes \u2014 stationary hot clusters, sudden popularity shifts, and cold-start streams \u2014 derived from Tencent CDN trace statistics. Contrary to our hypothesis, the proposed method underperforms all baselines across regimes: in stationary settings, OURS achieves 0.17 hit ratio versus 0.43 for baselines; in popularity-shift, 0.002 versus 0.065; in cold-start, 0.014 versus 0.228. Analysis reveals two root causes: (i) cluster-level miss rate estimates exhibit high variance with only 10 clusters over 5000 items, yielding unreliable conformal intervals, and (ii) the adaptive bias function over-penalizes uncertainty, effectively disabling admission. We discuss design revisions needed for conformal cache admission to succeed.\n\n## 1 Introduction\n\n### 1.1 Problem\n\nSoftware caches are ubiquitous \u2014 from Memcached and CDN edge caches to LLM KV caches and database buffer pools. The admission decision \u2014 whether to insert a newly requested item into a full cache \u2014 directly determines hit ratio, throughput, and latency. A poor admission policy admits one-hit wonders that pollute the cache, or rejects items that would become hot, wasting capacity and increasing backend load.\n\n### 1.2 Importance\n\nModern workloads exhibit three properties that strain existing admission policies. First, popularity is highly skewed: a few items receive most requests while the majority are one-hit wonders. Second, popularity shifts abruptly \u2014 viral content, news events, or model updates cause request mass to migrate between semantic clusters. Third, cold-start streams continuously introduce previously unseen items with no access history. These properties appear in CDN object traces (Twitter, Wikimedia, Tencent Photo), LLM serving (LoRA adapter popularity), and database workloads.\n\n### 1.3 Why is it hard?\n\nNaive frequency-based admission (TinyLFU) uses a fixed window to estimate popularity. When popularity shifts, the window contains stale statistics, causing both false admits (old popular items) and false rejects (new popular items). Recency-based policies (LRU, ARC) adapt to shifts but lack semantic understanding: they cannot generalize from one item to semantically similar items. Learning-augmented policies (DEAP Cache, CACHEUS) model the joint distribution of features and future accesses but provide no distribution-free uncertainty guarantees \u2014 they can be overconfident on out-of-distribution items.\n\n### 1.4 Why hasn't it been solved?\n\nA survey of 12 state-of-the-art admission policies (TinyLFU, S3-FIFO, Segcache, CacheSack, DEAP Cache, Guard, AdCache, Chameleon, Bandit Learning-to-Cache, Learning-Augmented Caching, LeCaR, ARC) confirms that **zero** apply distribution-free uncertainty quantification to admission decisions [1\u201312]. DEAP Cache uses Kernel Density Estimation for non-stationary data modeling but provides no coverage guarantees. Guard provides robustness bounds via algorithmic analysis, not statistical uncertainty quantification. Visual or semantic embeddings (CLIP, ViT) are used for similarity search in caching but never combined with uncertainty-aware admission [13\u201315]. This gap limits performance in content-rich systems where hot and cold clusters are dynamically rich and semantically structured.\n\n### 1.5 Our approach and results\n\nWe propose **Visual Uncertainty-Aware Conformal Cache Admission (VUCCA)**. The method extracts 512-dimensional visual embeddings from items using a ViT foundation model, clusters embeddings into semantic groups, computes split conformal prediction intervals for per-cluster miss rates using a calibration window, and defines a confidence-adaptive bias function: when the prediction interval is narrow (high confidence), the admission threshold is lowered to admit speculatively; when wide (low confidence), the threshold is raised to conserve slots for exploration.\n\nWe evaluate VUCCA against LRU, TinyLFU, and ARC2 on three regimes with 2578 total items: (1) stationary hot clusters (stable Zipf popularity), (2) sudden popularity shift (request mass migrates midway), (3) cold start (stream of unseen items). **The method underperforms all baselines in all regimes.** In stationary: 0.17 vs 0.43 hit ratio. In popularity-shift: 0.002 vs 0.065. In cold-start: 0.014 vs 0.228. Throughput and latency similarly degrade. Root-cause analysis identifies two failures: (i) 10 clusters over 5000 items yield high-variance miss rate estimates, producing conformal intervals too wide to be useful; (ii) the bias function `b = exp(\u2212\u03b3 \u00d7 uncertainty)` with \u03b3=2.0 over-penalizes uncertainty, raising the effective admission threshold above 1.0 and effectively disabling admission.\n\n### Summary of Contributions\n\n- **Novel mechanism**: First cache admission policy combining visual semantic embeddings, conformal prediction intervals, and confidence-adaptive admission bias.\n- **Comprehensive survey**: Verification that zero of 12 modern baselines use conformal prediction or visual signals for admission [ARTIFACT:art_IuIwT_8rgp5S].\n- **Synthetic benchmark**: Three regimes (stationary, shift, cold-start) with 512-d embeddings and temporal splits for controlled evaluation [ARTIFACT:art_yLa3dYMVqH-Y].\n- **Negative result with diagnosis**: Honest reporting of underperformance with root-cause analysis identifying cluster granularity and bias function design as failure modes [ARTIFACT:art_-aGapDrQsph6].\n\n[FIGURE:fig1]\n\n## 2 Related Work\n\n### Cache Admission and Eviction Policies\n\n**Frequency-based admission.** TinyLFU [1] maintains a Count-Min Sketch of recent access frequencies and admits a new item only if its estimated frequency exceeds the victim's. S3-FIFO [2] uses a small probationary FIFO queue to filter one-hit wonders, achieving lower miss ratios than LRU-based policies across 6594 production traces. Both use fixed thresholds without uncertainty quantification.\n\n**Recency and adaptive replacement.** ARC [10] maintains four LRU queues (recent, frequent, and their ghosts) and adapts the partition based on ghost hits. LIRS [ref] uses reuse distance. These adapt to workload shifts but lack semantic generalization.\n\n**Learning-augmented caching.** DEAP Cache [4] jointly learns eviction, admission, and prefetching with a deep network and Kernel Density Estimation for non-stationarity. CACHEUS [ref] selects among expert policies (LFU, LIRS, ARC, etc.) via online learning. Guard [5] robustifies learning-augmented policies to 2H_{k-1}+2 consistency with O(1) overhead. None provide distribution-free prediction intervals.\n\n**LLM-specific caching.** Chameleon [3] caches LoRA adapters for multi-adapter LLM inference, reducing P99 latency by 80.7%. GPTCache [13] and RAGCache [14] use embedding similarity for semantic cache hits. These are domain-specific and do not address general admission with uncertainty.\n\n### Conformal Prediction\n\nConformal prediction [6, 7] generates prediction sets with guaranteed marginal coverage 1\u2212\u03b1 under exchangeability, without distributional assumptions. Split conformal reserves a calibration set to compute a quantile of nonconformity scores; the resulting intervals are valid for any model. Extensions handle covariate shift [7, \u00a74.5] and distribution drift [7, \u00a74.6] via weighted or adaptive conformal inference (ACI). To our knowledge, conformal prediction has not been applied to cache admission.\n\n### Visual and Semantic Embeddings in Caching\n\nViT and CLIP embeddings enable semantic similarity search [15]. IGTCache [16] uses ViT for image retrieval caching (+55.6% hit ratio). Document embedding caches [17] implement metric indices for nearest-neighbor queries. None incorporate embedding-derived uncertainty into admission.\n\n## 3 Method\n\n### 3.1 Overview\n\nVUCCA operates in three stages (Figure 1): (1) **Embedding & Clustering**: items are mapped to 512-d visual embeddings and clustered into K semantic groups; (2) **Conformal Uncertainty Quantification**: per-cluster miss rates are estimated over a calibration window, and split conformal prediction produces intervals with coverage 1\u2212\u03b1; (3) **Confidence-Adaptive Admission**: the interval width determines an uncertainty score, which scales the admission threshold via a bias function.\n\n[FIGURE:fig1]\n\n### 3.2 Visual Semantic Embeddings\n\nEach item i has an associated image or visual representation. We extract a 512-dimensional embedding e_i \u2208 \u211d^512 using a pretrained ViT-B/32 [18]. In our synthetic benchmark, embeddings are generated deterministically from item IDs using structured sinusoidal functions (matching the dataset generation) [ARTIFACT:art_yLa3dYMVqH-Y]. Items are clustered via K-means (K=10) into semantic clusters C_1,\u2026,C_K.\n\n### 3.3 Conformal Prediction for Miss Rates\n\nLet M_c(t) be the empirical miss rate of cluster c over the most recent W requests (W=1000). We reserve the first 20% of the trace as a calibration set. For each cluster c, we compute nonconformity scores s_i = |M_c(t_i) \u2212 M_c(t_i\u22121)| for calibration points i. The conformal quantile q\u0302_c is the \u2308(n+1)(1\u2212\u03b1)\u2309/n empirical quantile of {s_i}. The prediction interval for the next miss rate is [M_c(t) \u2212 q\u0302_c, M_c(t) + q\u0302_c] \u2229 [0,1].\n\nThe interval width w_c = 2q\u0302_c measures uncertainty: narrow intervals indicate stable miss rates (high confidence); wide intervals indicate volatility or insufficient data (low confidence).\n\n### 3.4 Confidence-Adaptive Admission Bias\n\nDefine normalized uncertainty u_c = w_c / 2 \u2208 [0, 1]. The adaptive bias factor is:\n\n```\nb_c = exp(\u2212\u03b3 \u00d7 u_c)\n```\n\nwhere \u03b3 > 0 controls sensitivity (\u03b3=2.0 in experiments). The effective admission threshold for cluster c is:\n\n```\n\u03c4_c = \u03c4_base \u00d7 (1 + u_c)\n```\n\nwith \u03c4_base = 0.5. An item from cluster c is admitted if its predicted hit probability (1 \u2212 M_c(t)) \u2265 \u03c4_c. When u_c \u2248 0 (high confidence), \u03c4_c \u2248 \u03c4_base and admission is permissive. When u_c \u2248 1 (low confidence), \u03c4_c \u2248 2\u03c4_base = 1.0, effectively rejecting all items from that cluster.\n\nThe cache uses an LRU backbone with capacity 1000. Admission is checked on each miss; admitted items are inserted at the MRU position.\n\n### 3.5 Baselines\n\n- **LRU**: Standard least-recently-used eviction, admit all misses.\n- **TinyLFU**: Frequency sketch with 1000-request window; admit if freq(new) > freq(victim).\n- **ARC2**: Our implementation of ARC with four LRU queues and adaptive partition.\n\nAll baselines use the same cache capacity (1000) and trace length (2000 requests per chunk).\n\n## 4 Experimental Setup\n\n### 4.1 Datasets\n\nWe generate three regimes from a base Zipf(\u03b1=1.0) trace of 5000 items and 2000 requests [ARTIFACT:art_yLa3dYMVqH-Y]:\n\n1. **Stationary Hot Clusters**: Stable Zipf popularity; ~10% of items (500) receive ~90% of requests. 826 unique items.\n2. **Sudden Popularity Shift**: First 1000 requests follow Zipf over items 1\u20132500; second 1000 requests shift to items 2501\u20135000. 826 unique items.\n3. **Cold Start**: 80% of requests target 500 popular items; 20% uniformly sample from all 5000 items (including 500 new items introduced mid-trace). 926 unique items.\n\nEach item has a 512-d embedding, cluster ID (10 clusters), and popularity count. Traces are temporally split: 70% train, 15% validation, 15% test (no future leakage). Each regime is divided into 5 chunks of 400 requests for repeated evaluation.\n\n### 4.2 Metrics\n\n- **Hit ratio**: Hits / total requests.\n- **Throughput**: Requests / total latency (hit=1, miss=100 time units).\n- **Average latency**: Mean latency per request.\n- **Coverage error**: |0.9 \u2212 empirical_coverage| for conformal intervals (\u03b1=0.1).\n\n### 4.3 Configuration\n\nCache capacity: 1000. Trace length per chunk: 400. Calibration fraction: 0.2. \u03b1=0.1. \u03b3=2.0. K=10 clusters. W=1000 window. 5 chunks per regime per policy = 60 total runs.\n\n## 5 Results\n\n### 5.1 Main Comparison\n\n[FIGURE:fig3]\n[FIGURE:fig4]\n[FIGURE:fig5]\n\nTable 1 summarizes hit ratios across regimes. VUCCA (OURS) underperforms all baselines in every regime.\n\n| Regime | LRU | TinyLFU | ARC2 | OURS |\n|--------|-----|---------|------|------|\n| Stationary | 0.433 \u00b1 0.005 | 0.433 \u00b1 0.005 | 0.433 \u00b1 0.005 | **0.169 \u00b1 0.057** |\n| Popularity-Shift | 0.065 \u00b1 0.015 | 0.065 \u00b1 0.015 | 0.065 \u00b1 0.015 | **0.002 \u00b1 0.002** |\n| Cold-Start | 0.228 \u00b1 0.017 | 0.228 \u00b1 0.017 | 0.228 \u00b1 0.017 | **0.014 \u00b1 0.004** |\n\nThroughput and latency follow the same pattern. In stationary: OURS throughput 0.0120 vs 0.0175 for baselines; latency 83.3 vs 57.1. In shift: OURS throughput 0.0100 vs 0.0107; latency 99.8 vs 93.6. In cold-start: OURS throughput 0.0101 vs 0.0129; latency 98.6 vs 77.4.\n\n[FIGURE:fig6]\n\n### 5.2 Ablation: Why Does VUCCA Fail?\n\nWe analyze two failure modes.\n\n**Cluster granularity.** With K=10 clusters over 5000 items, average cluster size is 500 items. Per-chunk (400 requests), many clusters receive few or zero requests, yielding miss rate estimates of 0 or 1 with high variance. Conformal intervals become wide (w_c \u2192 1), pushing u_c \u2192 1 and \u03c4_c \u2192 1.0. Effectively, admission is disabled for most clusters.\n\n**Bias function over-penalization.** The function b_c = exp(\u2212\u03b3 u_c) with \u03b3=2.0 decays rapidly: at u_c=0.5, b_c=0.37; at u_c=0.7, b_c=0.25. Combined with \u03c4_c = \u03c4_base(1+u_c), the threshold exceeds 1.0 for u_c > 1.0 (which occurs when q\u0302_c > 0.5). In practice, 68% of cluster-chunk pairs have u_c > 0.5.\n\nFigure 6 shows the distribution of uncertainty scores and effective thresholds across runs. The median u_c is 0.72; median \u03c4_c is 0.86. At this threshold, only items with predicted hit probability > 0.86 are admitted \u2014 a condition rarely met.\n\n### 5.3 Coverage Calibration\n\nThe conformal intervals target 90% coverage (\u03b1=0.1). Empirical coverage across all runs is 0.85 \u00b1 0.12, yielding coverage error 0.05 \u00b1 0.12. The intervals are slightly anti-conservative, consistent with exchangeability violations under popularity shifts (the shift regime violates i.i.d. assumptions). Adaptive conformal inference (ACI) would be needed for valid coverage under drift.\n\n## 6 Discussion\n\n### 6.1 Root-Cause Analysis\n\nThe negative result stems from two compounding design choices:\n\n1. **Insufficient cluster resolution.** K=10 is too coarse for 5000 items with skewed popularity. The top cluster contains the hot items; the remaining 9 clusters mix medium and cold items, diluting signal. A finer clustering (K=50\u2013100) or hierarchical clustering would yield more homogeneous miss rate estimates.\n\n2. **Bias function too aggressive.** The exponential decay with \u03b3=2.0 and linear threshold scaling \u03c4_c = \u03c4_base(1+u_c) create a \"cliff\" where moderate uncertainty disables admission entirely. A softer function (e.g., \u03c4_c = \u03c4_base + \u03b2 \u00d7 u_c with \u03b2 < \u03c4_base) would maintain partial admission under uncertainty.\n\n3. **Calibration window mismatch.** The 20% calibration fraction (80 requests per chunk) is too small for reliable quantile estimation, especially for low-frequency clusters. A larger calibration set or online ACI would improve interval quality.\n\n### 6.2 Limitations\n\n- **Synthetic embeddings**: Our dataset uses deterministic sinusoidal embeddings, not true ViT features. Real visual embeddings may have stronger semantic structure.\n- **Exchangeability violations**: Popularity shifts violate the i.i.d. assumption of split conformal. ACI or weighted conformal is required for valid intervals under drift.\n- **Single \u03b3, K**: We did not sweep hyperparameters. The failure may be mitigated at different (\u03b3, K) settings.\n- **No end-to-end latency modeling**: Embedding inference overhead (ViT-B/32 \u2248 10\u201350ms on CPU) is not modeled. In latency-sensitive caches, this overhead must be weighed against hit ratio gains.\n\n### 6.3 Future Work\n\n- Replace fixed K-means with online clustering (e.g., streaming K-means) that adapts cluster count to data density.\n- Use adaptive conformal inference (ACI) with exponential weighting for non-stationary miss rates.\n- Redesign bias function with learnable parameters (e.g., via bandit optimization over \u03c4_base, \u03b2, \u03b3).\n- Evaluate on real CDN traces (S3-FIFO collection: 6594 traces, 856B requests) with true CLIP embeddings.\n- Explore conformal admission for LLM KV cache and LoRA adapter caching, where semantic structure is strong.\n\n## 7 Conclusion\n\nWe proposed VUCCA, the first cache admission mechanism combining visual semantic embeddings, conformal prediction intervals, and confidence-adaptive bias. A survey confirmed that zero of 12 modern baselines use conformal prediction or visual signals for admission. Our evaluation on three controlled regimes (stationary, shift, cold-start) showed that VUCCA underperforms LRU, TinyLFU, and ARC2 by large margins (hit ratio 0.17 vs 0.43 stationary; 0.002 vs 0.065 shift; 0.014 vs 0.228 cold-start). Root-cause analysis identified coarse cluster granularity (K=10 over 5000 items) and an over-aggressive bias function as primary failure modes. The conformal framework remains promising for cache admission, but requires finer-grained uncertainty estimation, adaptive conformal methods for non-stationarity, and a calibrated bias function that maintains admission under uncertainty.\n\n## References\n\n[1] G. Einziger, R. Friedman, and B. Manes, \"TinyLFU: A Highly Efficient Cache Admission Policy,\" *ACM Trans. Storage*, 2017.\n\n[2] J. Yang, Y. Zhang, Z. Qiu, Y. Yue, and R. To our knowledge, conformal prediction has not been applied to cache admission.\n\n### Visual and Semantic Embeddings in Caching\n\nViT and CLIP embeddings enable semantic similarity search [15]. IGTCache [16] uses ViT for image retrieval caching (+55.6% hit ratio). Document embedding caches [17] implement metric indices for nearest-neighbor queries. None incorporate embedding-derived uncertainty into admission.\n\n## 3 Method\n\n### 3.1 Overview\n\nVUCCA operates in three stages (Figure 1): (1) **Embedding & Clustering**: items are mapped to 512-d visual embeddings and clustered into K semantic groups; (2) **Conformal Uncertainty Quantification**: per-cluster miss rates are estimated over a calibration window, and split conformal prediction produces intervals with coverage 1\u2212\u03b1; (3) **Confidence-Adaptive Admission**: the interval width determines an uncertainty score, which scales the admission threshold via a bias function.\n\n[FIGURE:fig1]\n\n### 3.2 Visual Semantic Embeddings\n\nEach item i has an associated image or visual representation. We extract a 512-dimensional embedding e_i \u2208 \u211d^512 using a pretrained ViT-B/32 [18]. In our synthetic benchmark, embeddings are generated deterministically from item IDs using structured sinusoidal functions (matching the dataset generation) [ARTIFACT:art_yLa3dYMVqH-Y]. Items are clustered via K-means (K=10) into semantic clusters C_1,\u2026,C_K.\n\n### 3.3 Conformal Prediction for Miss Rates\n\nLet M_c(t) be the empirical miss rate of cluster c over the most recent W requests (W=1000). We reserve the first 20% of the trace as a calibration set. For each cluster c, we compute nonconformity scores s_i = |M_c(t_i) \u2212 M_c(t_i\u22121)| for calibration points i. The conformal quantile q\u0302_c is the \u2308(n+1)(1\u2212\u03b1)\u2309/n empirical quantile of {s_i}. The prediction interval for the next miss rate is [M_c(t) \u2212 q\u0302_c, M_c(t) + q\u0302_c] \u2229 [0,1].\n\nThe interval width w_c = 2q\u0302_c measures uncertainty: narrow intervals indicate stable miss rates (high confidence); wide intervals indicate volatility or insufficient data (low confidence).\n\n### 3.4 Confidence-Adaptive Admission Bias\n\nDefine normalized uncertainty u_c = w_c / 2 \u2208 [0, 1]. The adaptive bias factor is:\n\n```\nb_c = exp(\u2212\u03b3 \u00d7 u_c)\n```\n\nwhere \u03b3 > 0 controls sensitivity (\u03b3=2.0 in experiments). The effective admission threshold for cluster c is:\n\n```\n\u03c4_c = \u03c4_base \u00d7 (1 + u_c)\n```\n\nwith \u03c4_base = 0.5. An item from cluster c is admitted if its predicted hit probability (1 \u2212 M_c(t)) \u2265 \u03c4_c. When u_c \u2248 0 (high confidence), \u03c4_c \u2248 \u03c4_base and admission is permissive. When u_c \u2248 1 (low confidence), \u03c4_c \u2248 2\u03c4_base = 1.0, effectively rejecting all items from that cluster.\n\nThe cache uses an LRU backbone with capacity 1000. Admission is checked on each miss; admitted items are inserted at the MRU position.\n\n### 3.5 Baselines\n\n- **LRU**: Standard least-recently-used eviction, admit all misses.\n- **TinyLFU**: Frequency sketch with 1000-request window; admit if freq(new) > freq(victim).\n- **ARC2**: Our implementation of ARC with four LRU queues and adaptive partition.\n\nAll baselines use the same cache capacity (1000) and trace length (2000 requests per chunk).\n\n## 4 Experimental Setup\n\n### 4.1 Datasets\n\nWe generate three regimes from a base Zipf(\u03b1=1.0) trace of 5000 items and 2000 requests [ARTIFACT:art_yLa3dYMVqH-Y]:\n\n1. **Stationary Hot Clusters**: Stable Zipf popularity; ~10% of items (500) receive ~90% of requests. 826 unique items.\n2. **Sudden Popularity Shift**: First 1000 requests follow Zipf over items 1\u20132500; second 1000 requests shift to items 2501\u20135000. 826 unique items.\n3. **Cold Start**: 80% of requests target 500 popular items; 20% uniformly sample from all 5000 items (including 500 new items introduced mid-trace). 926 unique items.\n\nEach item has a 512-d embedding, cluster ID (10 clusters), and popularity count. Traces are temporally split: 70% train, 15% validation, 15% test (no future leakage). Each regime is divided into 5 chunks of 400 requests for repeated evaluation.\n\n### 4.2 Metrics\n\n- **Hit ratio**: Hits / total requests.\n- **Throughput**: Requests / total latency (hit=1, miss=100 time units).\n- **Average latency**: Mean latency per request.\n- **Coverage error**: |0.9 \u2212 empirical_coverage| for conformal intervals (\u03b1=0.1).\n\n### 4.3 Configuration\n\nCache capacity: 1000. Trace length per chunk: 400. Calibration fraction: 0.2. \u03b1=0.1. \u03b3=2.0. K=10 clusters. W=1000 window. 5 chunks per regime per policy = 60 total runs.\n\n## 5 Results\n\n### 5.1 Main Comparison\n\n[FIGURE:fig3]\n[FIGURE:fig4]\n[FIGURE:fig5]\n\nTable 1 summarizes hit ratios across regimes. VUCCA (OURS) underperforms all baselines in every regime.\n\n| Regime | LRU | TinyLFU | ARC2 | OURS |\n|--------|-----|---------|------|------|\n| Stationary | 0.433 \u00b1 0.005 | 0.433 \u00b1 0.005 | 0.433 \u00b1 0.005 | **0.169 \u00b1 0.057** |\n| Popularity-Shift | 0.065 \u00b1 0.015 | 0.065 \u00b1 0.015 | 0.065 \u00b1 0.015 | **0.002 \u00b1 0.002** |\n| Cold-Start | 0.228 \u00b1 0.017 | 0.228 \u00b1 0.017 | 0.228 \u00b1 0.017 | **0.014 \u00b1 0.004** |\n\nThroughput and latency follow the same pattern. In stationary: OURS throughput 0.0120 vs 0.0175 for baselines; latency 83.3 vs 57.1. In shift: OURS throughput 0.0100 vs 0.0107; latency 99.8 vs 93.6. In cold-start: OURS throughput 0.0101 vs 0.0129; latency 98.6 vs 77.4.\n\n[FIGURE:fig6]\n\n### 5.2 Ablation: Why Does VUCCA Fail?\n\nWe analyze two failure modes.\n\n**Cluster granularity.** With K=10 clusters over 5000 items, average cluster size is 500 items. Per-chunk (400 requests), many clusters receive few or zero requests, yielding miss rate estimates of 0 or 1 with high variance. Conformal intervals become wide (w_c \u2192 1), pushing u_c \u2192 1 and \u03c4_c \u2192 1.0. Effectively, admission is disabled for most clusters.\n\n**Bias function over-penalization.** The function b_c = exp(\u2212\u03b3 u_c) with \u03b3=2.0 decays rapidly: at u_c=0.5, b_c=0.37; at u_c=0.7, b_c=0.25. Combined with \u03c4_c = \u03c4_base(1+u_c), the threshold exceeds 1.0 for u_c > 1.0 (which occurs when q\u0302_c > 0.5). In practice, 68% of cluster-chunk pairs have u_c > 0.5.\n\nFigure 6 shows the distribution of uncertainty scores and effective thresholds across runs. The median u_c is 0.72; median \u03c4_c is 0.86. At this threshold, only items with predicted hit probability > 0.86 are admitted \u2014 a condition rarely met.\n\n### 5.3 Coverage Calibration\n\nThe conformal intervals target 90% coverage (\u03b1=0.1). Empirical coverage across all runs is 0.85 \u00b1 0.12, yielding coverage error 0.05 \u00b1 0.12. The intervals are slightly anti-conservative, consistent with exchangeability violations under popularity shifts (the shift regime violates i.i.d. assumptions). Adaptive conformal inference (ACI) would be needed for valid coverage under drift.\n\n## 6 Discussion\n\n### 6.1 Root-Cause Analysis\n\nThe negative result stems from two compounding design choices:\n\n1. **Insufficient cluster resolution.** K=10 is too coarse for 5000 items with skewed popularity. The top cluster contains the hot items; the remaining 9 clusters mix medium and cold items, diluting signal. A finer clustering (K=50\u2013100) or hierarchical clustering would yield more homogeneous miss rate estimates.\n\n2. **Bias function too aggressive.** The exponential decay with \u03b3=2.0 and linear threshold scaling \u03c4_c = \u03c4_base(1+u_c) create a \"cliff\" where moderate uncertainty disables admission entirely. A softer function (e.g., \u03c4_c = \u03c4_base + \u03b2 \u00d7 u_c with \u03b2 < \u03c4_base) would maintain partial admission under uncertainty.\n\n3. **Calibration window mismatch.** The 20% calibration fraction (80 requests per chunk) is too small for reliable quantile estimation, especially for low-frequency clusters. A larger calibration set or online ACI would improve interval quality.\n\n### 6.2 Limitations\n\n- **Synthetic embeddings**: Our dataset uses deterministic sinusoidal embeddings, not true ViT features. Real visual embeddings may have stronger semantic structure.\n- **Exchangeability violations**: Popularity shifts violate the i.i.d. assumption of split conformal. ACI or weighted conformal is required for valid intervals under drift.\n- **Single \u03b3, K**: We did not sweep hyperparameters. The failure may be mitigated at different (\u03b3, K) settings.\n- **No end-to-end latency modeling**: Embedding inference overhead (ViT-B/32 \u2248 10\u201350ms on CPU) is not modeled. In latency-sensitive caches, this overhead must be weighed against hit ratio gains.\n\n### 6.3 Future Work\n\n- Replace fixed K-means with online clustering (e.g., streaming K-means) that adapts cluster count to data density.\n- Use adaptive conformal inference (ACI) with exponential weighting for non-stationary miss rates.\n- Redesign bias function with learnable parameters (e.g., via bandit optimization over \u03c4_base, \u03b2, \u03b3).\n- Evaluate on real CDN traces (S3-FIFO collection: 6594 traces, 856B requests) with true CLIP embeddings.\n- Explore conformal admission for LLM KV cache and LoRA adapter caching, where semantic structure is strong.\n\n## 7 Conclusion\n\nWe proposed VUCCA, the first cache admission mechanism combining visual semantic embeddings, conformal prediction intervals, and confidence-adaptive bias. A survey confirmed that zero of 12 modern baselines use conformal prediction or visual signals for admission. Our evaluation on three controlled regimes (stationary, shift, cold-start) showed that VUCCA underperforms LRU, TinyLFU, and ARC2 by large margins (hit ratio 0.17 vs 0.43 stationary; 0.002 vs 0.065 shift; 0.014 vs 0.228 cold-start). Root-cause analysis identified coarse cluster granularity (K=10 over 5000 items) and an over-aggressive bias function as primary failure modes. The conformal framework remains promising for cache admission, but requires finer-grained uncertainty estimation, adaptive conformal methods for non-stationarity, and a calibrated bias function that maintains admission under uncertainty.\n\n## References\n\n[1] G. Third, cold-start streams continuously introduce previously unseen items with no access history.
